indiaMissions.title: Northeast India: Khasi, Naga and Mizo Christianity
indiaMissions.region: Meghalaya (Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills), Nagaland, Mizoram, Manipur, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh
indiaMissions.summary: In barely a century the hill peoples of India's northeast became the most Christian region of South Asia. Welsh Calvinistic Methodists among the Khasi (from 1841), American Baptists among the Garo and the Nagas (from the 1860s–70s), and Welsh Presbyterians and British Baptists among the Mizo (from 1894) gave these peoples Roman-script literacy, schools and hospitals; but the decisive growth came through indigenous evangelists and repeated revivals in the twentieth century. By the 2011 census Christians made up about 88% of Nagaland, 87% of Mizoram and 75% of Meghalaya.
indiaMissions.story:
Christianity reached the northeast at the edge of British expansion into the hills between Bengal, Assam and Burma. Serampore Baptists sent the Bengali evangelist Krishna Chandra Pal to the Khasi at Sohra (Cherrapunji) in 1813, and the American Baptist missionaries Nathan Brown and Oliver Cutter, who had come from the Burma mission, settled at Sadiya in upper Assam in 1836 hoping to reach the Shan and ultimately China. These early efforts produced little, but American Baptists moved to the Brahmaputra valley (Sibsagar, Nowgong, Gauhati) and found that the hill peoples, not the Hindu Assamese, responded. The Garo converts Omed and Ramkhe were baptised at Gauhati in 1863, and Garo evangelists, not foreigners, carried the faith into the Garo Hills, where Tura became the mission centre from 1877.

The Welsh Calvinistic Methodists (later the Presbyterian Church of Wales) chose the Khasi Hills as their first foreign field. Thomas Jones arrived at Sohra on 22 June 1841, devised a Roman-script orthography for Khasi, opened schools and printed the first Khasi books; the first converts were baptised in 1846. Under later Welsh missionaries the mission spread to Shillong, Jowai and the Jaintia (Pnar) country, and the Welsh Revival of 1904–05 was echoed in a Khasi revival in 1905–06 that swept the presbyteries. Catholics, especially the Salesians of Don Bosco who arrived in Shillong in 1922, later built a Catholic community of comparable size, so that Meghalaya today is divided chiefly between Presbyterians and Catholics, with Baptists dominant among the Garo.

Among the Nagas the breakthrough came through an Assamese convert, Godhula Rufus Brown, who in 1871–72 visited the Ao village of Dekahaimong (Molungkimong); in November 1872 Edward Winter Clark baptised nine Ao men at Sibsagar. Clark and his wife Mary Mead Clark settled among the Ao at Molung in 1876, translated scripture and hymns into Ao, and the mission later moved to Impur (1894). Other American Baptists opened work among the Angami at Kohima (C. D. King from 1881, the physician Sidney Rivenburg from 1887), the Lotha at Wokha and the Sema. Growth was slow until the 1930s–50s: Christians were a small minority of Nagas at Indian independence, but conversion accelerated sharply amid the upheavals of the Second World War, the Battle of Kohima (1944) and the Naga nationalist struggle, and was reinforced by revivals in the 1950s and in 1976. The Nagaland Baptist Church Council, organised in 1937 as the Naga Hills Baptist Church Council, now claims one of the largest concentrations of Baptists anywhere.

The Mizo (Lushai) Hills were annexed by the British only in 1890–91. Two Baptists sponsored by the Arthington Aborigines Mission, J. Herbert Lorrain and Frederick W. Savidge, arrived at Aizawl on 11 January 1894, reduced Lushai to writing in the Roman alphabet (the ‘A, AW, B’ primer) and translated Luke, John and Acts before leaving in 1897. The Welsh Calvinistic Methodist David Evan Jones arrived in Aizawl in August 1897 and Edwin Rowlands in 1898, while Lorrain and Savidge returned in 1903 for the Baptist Missionary Society to the south, based at Serkawn near Lunglei. The first Mizo converts, Khuma and Khara, were baptised in 1899. A series of revivals (1906, 1913, 1919, the 1930s) reshaped Mizo culture: indigenous hymns and dance-like worship (the ‘khuang’ drum) were adopted, the bachelors' dormitory (zawlbuk) disappeared, and within half a century almost the entire population was Christian, with literacy among the highest in India.

In Manipur William Pettigrew, who arrived in Imphal in 1894, was barred by the Maharaja and the colonial political agent from working among the Hindu Meitei of the valley and moved in 1896 to Ukhrul among the Tangkhul Nagas; the Welshman Watkin Roberts founded the Thadou-Kuki Pioneer Mission (1910) among the Kuki, Hmar and related peoples. The pattern repeated across the region: Hindu or Buddhist valley and plains peoples remained largely untouched, while animist hill peoples, under the pressure of colonial administration, the end of head-hunting and village warfare, and the arrival of schools and money economy, converted in group movements. Arunachal Pradesh, closed to missionaries until well after independence, saw rapid growth from the 1970s onward, largely through Nagas, Mizos and other northeastern evangelists.

Christianity became bound up with ethnic identity and politics. Angami Zapu Phizo's Naga National Council, many of whose leaders were Baptists, declared independence in 1947 and fought the Indian state from the 1950s; the slogan ‘Nagaland for Christ’ later became a political as well as religious claim. The Mizo National Front rebellion of 1966–86 under Laldenga brought the Indian Air Force's bombing of Aizawl in March 1966 and the forced regrouping of villages; churches acted as mediators and the Presbyterian and Baptist leadership helped secure the Mizo Peace Accord of 1986. Churches have also been accused of partisanship in elections and of failing to restrain ethnic violence, as in the expulsion of Bru (Reang) people from Mizoram after 1997 and the Meitei–Kuki-Zo conflict in Manipur from May 2023, in which hundreds of churches, temples and thousands of homes were destroyed.

Today the region's churches are among the most self-supporting and missionary-minded in India. Mizo Presbyterians and Naga Baptists send hundreds of missionaries to other parts of India and to neighbouring countries, sustained by systems of tithing and ‘handful of rice’ (buhfai tham) offerings pioneered by Mizo women. The northeast thus inverted the usual Indian pattern: here Christianity is a majority, tribal, largely Protestant faith rather than a minority of Dalits and Syrian Christians.

Mizo (Lushai) clans and related Hmar, Lai and Mara peoples, through Welsh Presbyterians in the north and British Baptists in the south.
Tangkhul Nagas, Kukis and other hill peoples of Manipur, through Pettigrew and the Thadou-Kuki (North East India General) Mission; the Hindu Meitei majority of the valley largely remained Hindu.

focus: Reducing unwritten hill languages to the Roman alphabet and translating scripture, hymns and primers.
Village schools, mission high schools and teacher training, which produced the region's first educated elite.
Training indigenous evangelists, pastors and teachers who carried the faith from village to village.
Medical work at stations such as Kohima, Jowai, Shillong and Durtlang (Aizawl).
Moral and social reform: discouraging rice beer, head-hunting, feasts of merit and traditional sacrifices.
Revival meetings, conventions and singing as the heart of church life.
strategies: Comity agreements dividing the region between missions (Welsh Presbyterians in the Khasi Hills and north Mizoram, Baptists in the Garo, Naga and south Mizo hills), which produced strong single-denomination identities.
Reliance on indigenous agents from the start — Garo, Assamese, Ao and Mizo evangelists did most of the pioneering.
Roman-script literacy deliberately chosen over Bengali or Assamese script, tying literacy to the mission school and the Bible.
Early self-support: tithing, the Mizo women's ‘handful of rice’ offering and village-supported pastors.
Working under colonial protection: the Inner Line (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873) excluded traders and settlers but admitted missionaries as agents of ‘civilisation’ in the hills.
Revival-based renewal, with indigenous hymnody and music replacing imported Welsh and American tunes in the twentieth century.
challenges: Extreme isolation, malaria and high missionary mortality in the early decades (Sadiya, Sohra, Molung).
Head-hunting, inter-village warfare and British punitive expeditions that made missionaries part of a violent colonial frontier.
Linguistic diversity: dozens of mutually unintelligible Naga and Kuki-Chin languages each needing separate translation.
Colonial restrictions: missionaries were kept out of Manipur valley and the Naga areas beyond administered territory, and much of Arunachal was closed until late in the twentieth century.
Insurgency and counter-insurgency after 1947 (Naga and Mizo conflicts), with army operations, village regrouping and church leaders caught between rebels and the state.
Denominational splits, revivalist sects and later Pentecostal and charismatic movements dividing the older churches.
harms: Missions condemned and helped dismantle institutions such as the Naga morung and Mizo zawlbuk (youth dormitories), feasts of merit, traditional festivals, songs and rice beer, causing a loss of oral heritage that churches have only recently tried to recover.

Close cooperation with colonial administrators — missionaries served as interpreters, recruited labour corps in the First World War and benefited from punitive pacification — tied the faith to British rule.
Strict comity created denominational monopolies and sometimes social pressure on dissenters; church discipline could be heavy-handed (fines, exclusion for drinking or traditional rites).

Christianity became fused with ethnic nationalism; churches have been accused of tolerating or legitimising insurgent violence and, later, of exclusion of non-Christian minorities such as the Bru of Mizoram.
In the Manipur conflict from 2023 and earlier Naga–Kuki clashes (1990s), Christian peoples fought each other along ethnic lines, exposing the limits of shared faith.
outcomes: Three Christian-majority states: Nagaland (about 88% in 2011), Mizoram (about 87%) and Meghalaya (about 75%), with large Christian minorities in Manipur (41%) and Arunachal Pradesh (30%).
Roman-script literary languages (Khasi, Garo, Ao, Mizo and others) and very high literacy, with Mizoram at about 91% in 2011.

Strong, self-governing churches — the Presbyterian Church of India (Khasi-Jaintia and Mizoram synods), the Nagaland Baptist Church Council, the Baptist Church of Mizoram, the Council of Baptist Churches in Northeast India — and a large Catholic presence.
Major missionary-sending churches that support hundreds of evangelists in other Indian states and abroad.
Churches acting as civic mediators in the Naga ceasefire process and the 1986 Mizo Peace Accord.
institutions: Presbyterian Church of India (Khasi-Jaintia Synod and Mizoram Synod), rooted in the Welsh mission.
Nagaland Baptist Church Council (1937) and the Council of Baptist Churches in Northeast India (1950).
Baptist Church of Mizoram (Serkawn) and Mizoram Presbyterian Church Synod (Aizawl).
St Edmund's College, St Anthony's College and other Catholic and Presbyterian colleges in Shillong, a regional centre of education.
Eastern Theological College, Jorhat (1905) and Aizawl Theological College.
Durtlang Presbyterian Hospital (Aizawl) and Christian hospitals at Jorhat, Shillong (Nazareth Hospital) and Kohima.
indiaMissions.legacy: Northeast India is the great exception in Indian Christianity: the only region where Christianity is the majority faith of whole peoples, adopted mostly in the twentieth century through indigenous evangelists, revivals and literacy rather than by colonial coercion. Its churches gave Khasi, Naga and Mizo peoples written languages and modern education, and they are now among India's most self-supporting and missionary-sending bodies, but the fusion of faith with tribal and national identity has also drawn the churches into insurgency, ethnic rivalry and the politics of the Indian frontier.

indiaMissions.title: Women's missions, Pandita Ramabai and the Mukti revival
indiaMissions.region: Maharashtra (Pune, Kedgaon, Bombay), Bengal, United Provinces (Lucknow), Madras Presidency
indiaMissions.summary: From the 1830s women's missionary societies sent single women to teach in girls' schools and visit secluded high-caste women in their homes (zenana work), and by 1900 women formed the majority of the Protestant missionary force. The most remarkable figure of this world was an Indian convert, the Sanskrit scholar Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), whose homes for widows and famine orphans at Pune and Kedgaon became the Mukti Mission and the setting of the 1905 Mukti revival, an early source of Indian Pentecostalism.
indiaMissions.story:
Missionary education for Indian girls began in the shadow of the men's missions: Hannah Marshman opened schools at Serampore in the early 1800s and Mary Ann Cooke (later Wilson) started girls' schools in Calcutta in 1822. The Society for Promoting Female Education in the East (1834) and the Indian Female Normal School Society (1852, later the Zenana Bible and Medical Mission) sent women teachers, and in Calcutta Hannah Catherine Mullens pioneered ‘zenana visiting’ in the 1850s, teaching reading and needlework — and the Bible — to secluded upper-caste women whom male missionaries could not meet. American women organised their own boards: the interdenominational Woman's Union Missionary Society (1861) and the Methodist Woman's Foreign Missionary Society (1869), which in 1870 sent Isabella Thoburn to Lucknow and the physician Clara Swain to Bareilly. The Church of England Zenana Missionary Society followed in 1880. By the end of the century women missionaries outnumbered men in most Protestant missions, and girls' schools, women's colleges and women's hospitals formed a large share of mission work.

Isabella Thoburn opened a school for six girls in a rented room in the Lucknow bazaar in 1870; it became the Lal Bagh school and, from 1886, the college that bears her name, one of the first Christian colleges for women in Asia. Its graduates and teachers included Lilavati Singh, who represented Indian women at international missionary gatherings. Indian Christian women became writers and reformers in their own right: Krupabai Satthianadhan wrote the first novels in English by an Indian woman (‘Kamala’ and ‘Saguna’, 1890s), Ellen Lakshmi Goreh wrote hymns, and the Sorabji sisters founded schools in Pune and, in Cornelia Sorabji's case, became India's first woman lawyer.

Pandita Ramabai was born Ramabai Dongre in 1858 into a Chitpavan Brahmin family; her father, unusually, taught his wife and daughter Sanskrit. After her parents and sister died in the famine of 1874–77 she and her brother wandered as reciters of the Puranas, and in Calcutta in 1878 the pandits gave her the titles ‘Pandita’ and ‘Sarasvati’. She married a Bengali lawyer of lower caste, Bipin Behari Medhvi, was widowed in 1882 with an infant daughter, Manorama, and moved to Pune, where she founded the Arya Mahila Samaj and gave evidence to the Hunter Education Commission. In 1883 she went to England with the help of the Anglican Community of St Mary the Virgin at Wantage, where she was baptised; but she resisted the sisters' attempts to make her an orthodox Anglican, insisting on her own reading of scripture and her Indian identity. In the United States (1886–88) she published ‘The High-Caste Hindu Woman’ (1887), a powerful indictment of child marriage and the treatment of widows, and organised Ramabai Associations to fund a school for widows.

Her Sharada Sadan (Home of Learning) opened in Bombay on 11 March 1889 and moved to Pune in 1890, run on officially non-sectarian lines with support from Hindu reformers. When several widows chose baptism, the nationalist press led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak's ‘Kesari’ accused her of proselytising under false pretences, and in 1893 most Hindu members of the advisory committee resigned and many pupils were withdrawn. After an evangelical conversion experience in 1891 Ramabai moved towards open evangelism. During the famine of 1896–97 she travelled into the Central Provinces and brought back several hundred destitute girls and women, and later others from the Gujarat famine of 1900; she built Mukti Sadan (House of Salvation) on land at Kedgaon, east of Pune, together with Kripa Sadan for ‘fallen’ women and homes for the blind. By 1900 about 1,500 women and girls lived at Mukti, with farms, a printing press, weaving and other industries.

From January 1905, after Ramabai had heard of the Welsh and Khasi revivals, prayer circles of hundreds of Mukti girls met daily; on 29–30 June 1905 a revival broke out marked by confession of sin, weeping, visions, ecstatic prayer and, by late 1906, speaking in tongues. Bands of young women went out to preach in surrounding villages. The American Methodist Minnie Abrams, Ramabai's co-worker, described it in ‘The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire’ (1906), which circulated in the United States and Chile, and the Mukti revival became one of the earliest sources of Pentecostalism independent of Azusa Street. Ramabai herself remained cautious about tongues as a necessary sign.

In her last decades Ramabai learned Greek and Hebrew and translated the whole Bible into simple Marathi, finishing the proofs shortly before her death on 5 April 1922; Manorama had died the previous year. The British government awarded her the Kaiser-i-Hind medal in 1919, and India issued a postage stamp in her honour in 1989. Feminist historians now see her as one of the foremost Indian social reformers of the nineteenth century, while evangelicals remember her as a revivalist and Bible translator; she herself refused to fit either the Brahmin reformist or the Western missionary mould. The Mukti Mission continues at Kedgaon, caring for women and children.

indiaMissions.legacy: Women's missions turned female education from a curiosity into an expectation in many Indian communities and gave Indian Christian women public roles decades before most of their contemporaries. Pandita Ramabai stands at the centre of that story: a Brahmin scholar who became a Christian without becoming a Westerner, a reformer whose critique of caste and patriarchy was sharpened by her faith, and the leader of a revival that fed the global Pentecostal movement. Her life also shows the costs of conversion in colonial India, where every school and shelter was read as part of a struggle over religion and nation.

indiaMissions.title: Medical missions: Clara Swain, Ida Scudder (Vellore), Ludhiana, Miraj
indiaMissions.region: Across India; major centres at Vellore (Tamil Nadu), Ludhiana (Punjab), Miraj (Maharashtra), Bareilly (Uttar Pradesh), Srinagar (Kashmir) and Guntur (Andhra Pradesh)
indiaMissions.summary: Medical missions grew from a handful of missionary doctors in the early nineteenth century into a vast network of hospitals, dispensaries, leprosy homes, nursing schools and medical colleges. Women doctors were decisive: Clara Swain (Bareilly, 1870), Edith Brown (Ludhiana, 1894) and Ida Scudder (Vellore, 1900) reached secluded women whom male doctors could not treat and trained the first generations of Indian women doctors and nurses. Christian Medical College Vellore and Christian Medical College Ludhiana remain among India's leading medical institutions.
indiaMissions.story:
John Thomas, the surgeon who sailed with William Carey in 1793, was the first Protestant medical missionary in Bengal, but systematic medical mission began with the American physician John Scudder, who went to Ceylon in 1819 and moved to Madras in 1836. His descendants — more than forty Scudders served in India over four generations — became the founding dynasty of medical mission in the Arcot region. Through the nineteenth century missions attached dispensaries to mission stations, convinced that healing was both Christ-like compassion and an effective way to gain a hearing; the CMS hospital in Srinagar, founded by Robert Elmslie in 1864–65 and later run by Arthur and Ernest Neve, became famous across the northern frontier.

The seclusion of women created the strongest argument for women doctors. In 1869 the Methodist Woman's Foreign Missionary Society sent Clara Swain, a graduate of the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, who reached Bareilly in January 1870 as the first fully qualified woman medical missionary in Asia. She began training a class of Indian girls in medicine, and the Nawab of Rampur gave land on which a women's hospital opened in 1874 — now the Clara Swain Hospital. Anna Kugler (Lutheran, Guntur, 1883), Fanny Butler (CEZMS, Kashmir and Bhagalpur, 1880s) and Elizabeth Bielby of Lucknow followed; Bielby carried a message from the Maharani of Panna to Queen Victoria in 1881, which led to the secular Countess of Dufferin's Fund (1885) for medical aid to Indian women.

In Ludhiana the English doctor Edith Brown founded the North India School of Medicine for Christian Women in 1894, training Indian women as doctors, compounders and nurses; it became the Christian Medical College Ludhiana and admitted men from 1964. In the Deccan the American Presbyterian William Wanless opened a hospital at Miraj in 1894 and trained Indian medical assistants there; the Miraj mission hospital became a major surgical centre in western India and Wanless was knighted in 1928. Leprosy work grew from the Mission to Lepers founded in 1874 by Wellesley Bailey after his experience at Ambala; mission leprosy homes at Purulia, Chandkhuri and elsewhere were for decades almost the only care available, and mission sanatoria such as the Union Mission Tuberculosis Sanatorium at Arogyavaram (1915) pioneered TB treatment.

Ida Sophia Scudder, granddaughter of John Scudder, was born at Ranipet in 1870. Visiting her parents in 1890, she was called in one night to three women dying in childbirth whose husbands refused a male doctor; all three died, and she resolved to study medicine, graduating from Cornell in 1899 in one of the first classes to admit women. She returned in 1900, opened a one-bed dispensary in Vellore and in 1902 the 40-bed Mary Taber Schell Memorial Hospital. From 1906 she ran roadside clinics by bullock cart and then motor car, started a nursing school (1909) and in 1918 opened the Missionary Medical School for Women, which received over 150 applications in its first year; the first class graduated in 1922 with notable success in the Madras government examinations. Supported by a growing union of missions in Britain and America, the school became Christian Medical College, granting Madras University degrees from 1942 and admitting men from 1947.

After independence medical missions faced the withdrawal of foreign personnel, rising costs and competition from government services. Vellore absorbed international talent such as the surgeon Paul Brand, who from 1947 developed reconstructive hand surgery for leprosy at Vellore and Karigiri (1955), and trained Indian specialists such as Mary Verghese, a paraplegic surgeon who pioneered rehabilitation medicine. Many smaller mission hospitals closed or struggled; others joined networks such as the Christian Medical Association of India (founded 1905) and the Emmanuel Hospital Association (1970), which took over mission hospitals across north India. Christian hospitals remain a significant part of Indian non-profit healthcare, especially in rural areas.

Medical mission was never only humanitarian. Waiting-room preaching, Bible readings before treatment and the expectation of a hearing in return for care were standard for much of the period, and Hindu and Muslim critics saw hospitals as instruments of conversion. Missionary medicine also disparaged Ayurvedic and Unani practitioners and traditional midwives, and leprosy asylums segregated patients in ways that later medicine regretted. Yet the hospitals, nursing schools and medical colleges trained thousands of Indian women and men at a time when few other routes into professional medicine existed for them.

indiaMissions.title: Amy Carmichael and Dohnavur
indiaMissions.summary: Amy Carmichael (1867–1951), an Ulster-born missionary sent by the Keswick Convention, worked in South India for fifty-five years without returning home. From 1901 she sheltered girls at risk of dedication as temple servants (devadasis), and her community at Dohnavur, formalised as the Dohnavur Fellowship in 1927, grew into a large children's home, school and hospital. Her many devotional books made her one of the most widely read missionary writers of the twentieth century, while her methods and claims have been debated.
indiaMissions.story:
Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born in 1867 at Millisle, County Down, into a Presbyterian mill-owning family. In Belfast she started work among the ‘shawlies’, girls employed in the mills, and through Robert Wilson, a founder of the Keswick Convention, she absorbed Keswick holiness teaching on surrender and the ‘victorious life’. In 1892 she became the first missionary supported by the Keswick Convention's mission fund. After a short and unhappy period in Japan (1893–94) and in Ceylon she went to India under the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, arriving in November 1895, and after language study in Bangalore joined the CMS missionary Thomas Walker in the Tirunelveli district.

Carmichael adopted Indian dress, stained her skin with coffee to pass in villages, and formed the ‘Starry Cluster’, a band of Indian Christian women — among them the widow Ponnammal — who travelled with her through the villages of the Tamil south preaching to women. Her first book, ‘Things as They Are: Mission Work in Southern India’ (1903), deliberately broke with the cheerful tone of missionary reports by describing hardness of heart, caste pressure and the sufferings of converts; mission supporters at first found it too bleak to publish.

On 6 March 1901 a seven-year-old girl named Preena escaped from a temple at Tiruvannamalai to which she had been given and found her way to Carmichael at Pannaivilai. Her account convinced Carmichael that girls were being dedicated to temples as devadasis and exploited sexually, and from then on she gave herself to rescuing children at risk. That year she settled at Dohnavur, a Christian village founded in the 1820s under Rhenius and named after a Prussian benefactor, Count Dohna. The first infants were brought in from 1904, and over the following decades the community took in hundreds of girls and, from 1918, boys as well. Children were brought up in family-like ‘nurseries’ under Indian ‘accals’ (elder sisters), with schooling, Tamil Christian worship and a strict, disciplined community life.

In 1916 Carmichael formed the Sisters of the Common Life, a group of Indian and European women committed to celibacy and service; in 1927 the work was formally constituted as the Dohnavur Fellowship, independent of any missionary society. A hospital, the ‘Place of Heavenly Healing’, was built from the late 1920s and served the surrounding villages. Carmichael never took a furlough and was known to the children as ‘Amma’. In 1931 she fell into a pit and was badly injured, and she spent most of her last twenty years as an invalid in her room, writing: she produced some thirty-five books of devotion, verse and narrative, including ‘Gold Cord’ (1932) and ‘If’ (1938), which shaped evangelical spirituality in Britain and North America.

Her work was controversial. Her claims about the scale of temple trafficking were questioned by some contemporaries, and she was accused of abduction; on at least one occasion she faced criminal proceedings over a girl she had hidden from relatives, which were eventually dropped. Critics saw Dohnavur as a closed world that cut children off from their families and culture, and Carmichael's autocratic leadership and refusal of outside oversight caused friction with the CMS and the CEZMS. At the same time her campaigning contributed to public pressure against temple dedication, which the Madras legislature outlawed in the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947, months after independence.

Carmichael died at Dohnavur on 18 January 1951 and was buried in the community garden under a bird-bath marked simply ‘Amma’. After her death the Fellowship passed gradually into Indian leadership and continues as an Indian-led body, caring for girls and elderly members of the family, running schools and a hospital. Elisabeth Elliot's biography ‘A Chance to Die’ (1987) made her a heroine of a new generation of evangelicals.

indiaMissions.legacy: Amy Carmichael is among the best-known women in the history of missions in India, remembered for her devotion, her refusal to return home and her protection of vulnerable children. Dohnavur survived her because Indian women had always done much of the work, and it continues under Indian leadership.

indiaMissions.title: Indian Christian thinkers: Tilak, Upadhyay, Sundar Singh, the Rethinking group
indiaMissions.region: Bengal, Maharashtra, Punjab and the Himalaya, Madras Presidency

place.name: Madras (Chennai), home of the Rethinking group

indiaMissions.summary: From the 1830s converts from high-caste Hindu and Sikh backgrounds began to interpret Christ in Indian categories: Krishna Mohan Banerjea read the Vedas as preparation for the gospel, Nehemiah Goreh refuted Hindu philosophy from within, Brahmabandhab Upadhyay tried to be a ‘Hindu-Catholic’ using Vedanta, Narayan Vaman Tilak wrote Marathi bhakti hymns, Sadhu Sundar Singh lived as a Christian sannyasi, and the Madras ‘Rethinking group’ (1938) challenged missionary forms of the church. Together they laid the foundations of Indian Christian theology.
indiaMissions.story:
The first generation of Indian Protestant intellectuals came from Alexander Duff's English school in Calcutta. Krishna Mohan Banerjea, a Kulin Brahmin radical of the Young Bengal circle, was baptised in 1832 and ordained an Anglican priest; in ‘The Arian Witness’ (1875) and later works he argued that the Vedic sacrifice of Prajapati foreshadowed Christ, an early ‘fulfilment’ theology. Nehemiah (Nilakantha) Goreh, a Chitpavan Brahmin from Benares baptised in 1848, wrote ‘A Rational Refutation of the Hindu Philosophical Systems’ (1862), joined the Anglican Society of St John the Evangelist, and influenced the conversion of Pandita Ramabai. Outside the churches, Rammohun Roy's ‘Precepts of Jesus’ (1820) and Keshub Chunder Sen's lectures on the ‘Oriental Christ’ showed Hindu reformers admiring Jesus while rejecting the missions.

Brahmabandhab Upadhyay (born Bhabani Charan Banerji, 1861) moved from the Brahmo Samaj to Anglican baptism and then, in 1891, to the Catholic Church. Taking the dress of a sannyasi in 1894, he called himself a Hindu by birth and culture and a Catholic by faith, and in his journal ‘Sophia’ and hymns such as ‘Vande Saccidanandam’ he proposed that Advaita Vedanta could serve Indian Christianity as Aristotle had served Thomas Aquinas, with Brahman understood as Sat-Chit-Ananda (being, consciousness, bliss) and so as Trinity. His plan for a Catholic monastery (matha) for Indian ascetics was blocked by the apostolic delegate. Turning to nationalism, he edited the Bengali daily ‘Sandhya’ during the agitation against the partition of Bengal; arrested for sedition in 1907, he died in hospital before his trial ended. Rejected by church authorities in his lifetime, he later became a patron of Catholic inculturation and the ashram movement.

In western India Narayan Vaman Tilak (1861–1919), a Chitpavan Brahmin poet, was baptised in Bombay in 1895 and worked with the American Marathi Mission at Ahmednagar. He wrote hundreds of Marathi hymns in the abhang and other forms of the Varkari bhakti poets, which remain the core of Marathi Christian worship. In 1917 he gave up his mission salary to found ‘God's Darbar’, a brotherhood of baptised and unbaptised disciples of Christ, arguing that Indians must be free to follow Christ without adopting a foreign church. His wife Lakshmibai Tilak, who followed him into the faith after a painful separation, wrote the Marathi autobiography ‘Smriti Chitre’, a classic of Marathi literature.

Sundar Singh (1889–c.1929), born into a Sikh family at Rampur in Ludhiana district, had a vision of Christ on 18 December 1904 after burning a Bible in anger; disowned by his family, he was baptised in the Anglican church at Simla on 3 September 1905. He chose to live as a wandering sadhu in a saffron robe, preaching in the Punjab, the Himalaya and Tibet, and from 1918 to 1922 travelled through South India, Asia, Europe, Australia and America, where crowds saw him as an ‘Indian St Francis’. His teaching was simple, mystical and parable-filled; critics, including the Jesuit Father Hosten and the Swiss pastor Oskar Pfister, questioned the historicity of his miracle stories and Tibetan adventures, while Streeter and Appasamy's study ‘The Sadhu’ (1921) defended him. He disappeared on a journey into Tibet in 1929.

In Madras a group of lay intellectuals — the judge Pandipeddi Chenchiah, the lawyer and later mayor of Madras Vengal Chakkarai, and others including A. N. Sudarisanam, G. V. Job and D. M. Devasahayam — had formed the Christo Samaj (1919) to promote Indian Christian independence. When the International Missionary Council met at Tambaram in 1938, Hendrik Kraemer's preparatory book ‘The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World’ insisted on the radical discontinuity between the gospel and all religions. The group replied with ‘Rethinking Christianity in India’ (1938), arguing that the raw fact of Christ, not Western church dogma or institutions, was what India needed, that Hinduism could serve as an ‘Old Testament’, and that the church in India was too dependent on mission money and forms. A. J. Appasamy developed a bhakti theology of union with Christ in the Johannine writings and became a bishop of the Church of South India; Christian ashrams such as Christukula (Tirupattur, 1921) and Christa Prema Seva (Pune, 1927) tried to embody Indian forms of community.

After independence, P. D. Devanandan and M. M. Thomas, through the Christian Institute for the Study of Religion and Society (1957), turned Indian Christian thought towards dialogue with secular nationalism, Hindu renaissance and social justice, and later Dalit theologians criticised the earlier thinkers for drawing so heavily on Brahmanical traditions that most Indian Christians, who were Dalit or tribal, did not share. The pioneers nevertheless showed that Christianity could be thought and sung in Indian idioms rather than only translated from Europe.

indiaMissions.title: V. S. Azariah, the Indian Missionary Society and the National Missionary Society
indiaMissions.region: Tirunelveli (Tamil Nadu), Dornakal and the Telugu country (Telangana, Andhra Pradesh), with national work across India
indiaMissions.summary: At the start of the twentieth century Indian Christians began founding their own missions. The Indian Missionary Society of Tinnevelly (1903) and the National Missionary Society (1905), both inspired by the young YMCA secretary V. S. Azariah, sent Indian missionaries with Indian money under Indian leadership. Azariah himself went as an IMS missionary to Dornakal and in 1912 became the first Indian bishop of the Anglican Church in India, presiding over a mass movement of Dalits and low-caste Telugus that brought roughly 200,000 people into the church and helping to create the Church of South India.
indiaMissions.story:
By 1900 Indian Christians had been criticising missionary control for decades. Independent bodies such as the Hindu Church of Lord Jesus (Tirunelveli, 1858), the National Church of India (Madras, 1886) and Kali Charan Banerji's Christo Samaj in Calcutta (1887) had tried to break free, and the Mar Thoma Syrian Church's Evangelistic Association (1888) and Maramon Convention (1895) showed the energy of Kerala's Syrian Christians. The decisive initiative came from a young Tamil Anglican of the Nadar community, Vedanayagam Samuel Azariah, born in 1874 at Vellalanvilai in Tirunelveli district, the son of a village priest. Educated at CMS schools and Madras Christian College, he became a travelling secretary of the YMCA from 1895, working with the American student leaders Sherwood Eddy and John R. Mott.

On 12 February 1903 Azariah and fellow Tirunelveli Christians founded the Indian Missionary Society of Tinnevelly at Palayamkottai, the first Protestant missionary society in India run entirely by Indians. Its chosen field was Dornakal, in the Telugu-speaking territories of the Nizam of Hyderabad, and its first missionaries went there in the following years. On Christmas Day 1905, in William Carey's library at Serampore, Azariah and leaders from across India founded the National Missionary Society with the motto ‘Indian men, Indian money and Indian leadership’. The NMS, interdenominational in scope, opened fields in the Punjab (Montgomery district), North Arcot and later other regions, and its general secretary K. T. Paul became one of the most respected Indian Christian public figures.

At the World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh in 1910 Azariah, one of the very few Asian delegates, gave the speech that made him famous: missionaries had given their goods and their lives for India, he said, but they had withheld friendship — ‘You have given your goods to feed the poor. You have given your bodies to be burned. We also ask for love. Give us friends!’ He had by then left the YMCA, been ordained (1909) and gone to Dornakal himself as an IMS missionary. On 29 December 1912 he was consecrated bishop of the new diocese of Dornakal in St Paul's Cathedral, Calcutta — the first Indian bishop of the Anglican Church in India — despite opposition from missionaries who doubted that an Indian could lead Europeans.

Dornakal became the scene of one of the largest Christian mass movements in India. Malas and Madigas, the main Dalit communities of the Telugu country, joined the church village by village; from the 1920s growing numbers of Sudra caste peasants followed. Azariah insisted that converts be well taught before baptism, that each village congregation support its own teacher-catechist, that every baptised Christian lay hands on his or her own head and say ‘Woe is me if I preach not the gospel’, and that Indian customs be adopted in worship. The Cathedral of the Epiphany at Dornakal, built over more than two decades, mixed Hindu and Islamic architectural motifs. His wife Anbu Mariammal led work among women. By his death on 1 January 1945, the movements he inspired had brought roughly 200,000 people into the church.

Azariah also chaired the National Christian Council and was a principal architect of the negotiations that produced the Church of South India in 1947, uniting Anglicans with Methodists, Presbyterians and Congregationalists. His advocacy of mass conversion brought him into conflict with M. K. Gandhi, who in the 1930s denounced conversions of the ‘untouchables’ as a spiritual and political threat, especially after B. R. Ambedkar's 1935 announcement that he would leave Hinduism; Gandhi is reported to have called Azariah his ‘enemy number one’. Azariah, for his part, opposed separate electorates for Christians and supported Indian self-rule while maintaining a close relationship with the British church.

The IMS and NMS survive as Indian mission agencies, and Azariah's principles — indigenous leadership, self-support, lay evangelism and church union — became the common sense of Indian Protestantism after independence. Critics have noted that the Dornakal movement left caste distinctions intact within congregations, with Mala, Madiga and Sudra Christians often worshipping separately, and that Azariah's moderate politics made him suspect to nationalists. His life nonetheless marked the moment when Indian Christians took charge of mission in their own country.

indiaMissions.summary: Indian Pentecostalism grew from the Mukti revival of 1905 and the arrival of Azusa Street missionaries in 1906–07, but took root above all through Indian leaders in Kerala and Tamil Nadu: K. E. Abraham's Indian Pentecostal Church of God, Pastor Paul's Ceylon Pentecostal Mission (The Pentecostal Mission), the Assemblies of God and the Church of God. Spreading among Syrian Christians, Dalits and later in the north, Pentecostal and charismatic churches are now the fastest-growing part of Indian Christianity, with millions of adherents, many in independent churches the census does not count separately.
indiaMissions.story:
South India had seen revivals with ecstatic features long before Azusa Street. In 1860 the Tamil evangelist John Christian Aroolappen, a disciple of the Brethren pioneer Anthony Norris Groves, reported prophecy and speaking in tongues in Tirunelveli, and the revival spread to Travancore; Kerala experienced further revivals in the 1870s, including the millenarian ‘Six Years' Party’ of Justus Joseph. In 1905 the revival at Pandita Ramabai's Mukti Mission near Pune, and by late 1906 its reports of tongues, made India one of the original centres of the twentieth-century Pentecostal movement. Minnie Abrams' account of Mukti was read in America and Chile.

Azusa Street sent Alfred G. Garr and his wife Lillian, who arrived in Calcutta at the end of 1906 and held meetings at the Bow Bazar Baptist chapel early in 1907. Garr had expected that tongues would give missionaries foreign languages for preaching; when this proved not to be so, he and others reinterpreted tongues as prayer language, a turning point in Pentecostal theology. Max Wood Moorhead in Bombay published reports of Pentecost in India, Thomas Ball Barratt visited in 1908, and George Berg brought the message to Travancore in 1909. The most important foreign worker in Kerala was Robert F. Cook, an American who arrived in 1913 and from 1914 worked from Mulakuzha; his mission affiliated with the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) in 1936. American Assemblies of God missionaries worked in Travancore from the 1920s and in the north from the 1910s.

Indian leaders soon led the movement. K. E. Abraham, a Syrian Christian schoolteacher, worked with Cook in the 1920s but in 1930 led most Indian believers out of the foreign-funded mission to build a self-supporting church; the Indian Pentecostal Church of God, which traces its beginnings to 1924, was registered in 1935 and made its headquarters at Kumbanad. Splits produced further bodies, notably the Sharon Fellowship Church under P. J. Thomas in 1953. Pastor Paul, a Hindu convert from Kerala, founded the Ceylon Pentecostal Mission in Colombo in 1923 with Alwin R. de Alwis; known in India as The Pentecostal Mission, it became famous for its celibate ministers dressed in white, communal ‘faith homes’, refusal of medicine and strict separation from the world, and spread through Tamil Nadu and Kerala with its headquarters later in Chennai.

Pentecostalism in Kerala drew converts from the Syrian Christian and Anglican (CSI) churches, which accused it of ‘sheep-stealing’, and from Dalit communities attracted by healing, exorcism and a message of equality before the Spirit. Caste nevertheless reproduced itself: Syrian Christian families largely controlled leadership, Dalit Pentecostals complained of segregated seating, separate burial and exclusion from office, and some churches divided along caste lines, such as the Church of God in Kerala, which split in 1972 into a largely Syrian ‘Kerala Division’ and a largely Dalit ‘Kerala State’ church. Kerala Pentecostals in turn became major missionaries to North India and the Gulf.

From the 1970s healing evangelists and charismatic movements spread the Pentecostal style far beyond Kerala. D. G. S. Dhinakaran's ‘Jesus Calls’ ministry (from 1970s Chennai) reached millions by prayer towers, radio and television; independent churches multiplied in Hyderabad, Bangalore, Mumbai and Delhi; and from the 2000s Pentecostal ‘ministries’ grew rapidly among Dalit and other poor communities in Punjab, often led by charismatic healers. Catholic charismatic renewal, especially the Divine Retreat Centre at Muringoor (Kerala), mirrored the same spirituality. Some of these movements attracted scandal: the Punjab pastor Bajinder Singh was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2025 for rape, and others have faced charges of fraudulent healing and financial abuse.

Pentecostals are now often at the centre of controversies over conversion. Hindu nationalist groups accuse them of aggressive proselytism, inducement by promises of healing and denigration of Hindu deities, and they have been disproportionately targeted in violence and in prosecutions under state anti-conversion laws. Their growth has made Indian Christianity more lay-led, more independent and more working-class, and has shifted its centre of energy from the historic denominations towards thousands of small congregations, many of which the census and most church statistics do not separately record.

indiaMissions.legacy: Indian Pentecostalism shows the indigenous energy of Indian Christianity. It began in an Indian women's revival at Mukti, was soon led by Indians and spread mainly through ordinary believers. It has given Dalits and the poor a religion of healing, dignity and lay leadership, while repeating the caste divisions of the older churches and producing schisms and scandals. Pentecostals are now the most visible Christians in many parts of India and are at the centre of the national dispute over conversion.
